== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low-to-moderate concern (incomplete docket access rather than case drop-out): all three selected lawsuits were tracked from filing (1999 or 2006) through judicial archiving (Aquidauana in June 2012; Santa Maria in December 2012) or ongoing execution (Tubarão through March 2018), but restricted public access to full party filings on the TJMS and TJRS websites created missing documentary evidence during the enforcement phase.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: the descriptive chronicle design lacks unlitigated comparator municipalities and cannot separate the effect of judicial orders from concurrent institutional, political, and financial drivers (e.g., the 2011 30-year SANESUL concession renewal in Aquidauana, 2015 municipalization politics in Santa Maria, environmental licensing via FATMA in Tubarão, and utility investment schedules), making causal assertions—such as claiming Tubarão's 2018 works occurred solely due to the lawsuit—unverified.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Strong: constitutional competencies, federal sanitation and procedural statutes (Law 11.445/2007, Law 7.347/1995, CPC art. 794, I), and case-specific litigation milestones (filing, first-instance sentences, appellate acórdãos, astreintes, prosecutorial motions, and execution/archiving orders) are documented with exact docket numbers, dates, and verbatim judicial excerpts across three courts (TJMS, TJRS, TRF4).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: formal procedural trajectories are directly verified from official court portals, whereas real-world sanitation implementation is assessed via heterogeneous secondary sources (union, municipal, and concessionaire press releases) rather than standardized engineering or household-level data, and in Santa Maria compliance in December 2012 is inferred solely from the docket's archiving entry without independent physical verification.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate: triangulation with local news and concessionaire announcements effectively exposes major gaps between formal judicial compliance and actual sewerage coverage in Aquidauana (15% coverage reported in August 2011 despite judicial extinction declaring full city sewage treatment) and Tubarão (zero implementation by early 2018 and a downscaled Phase 1 network), but relies on unverified secondary announcements and lacks standardized physical service metrics.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: no pre-specified protocol, extraction form, or coding rubric is reported, and the paper synthesizes unpublished 2016 undergraduate research chronicles in a personalized narrative style; however, the authors candidly report null/contrary observations, including Santa Maria's eventual compliance and Barcellos (2014)'s finding of no faster service delivery in litigated cases.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: only 3 public civil actions were examined out of the 258 sanitation lawsuits mapped in Barcellos (2014); although described colloquially as random ("aleatória"), no randomization procedure or sampling frame is reported, all 3 cases are plaintiff-favorable rulings from Southern and Center-West Brazil studied by a 2016 UERJ undergraduate group, creating substantial risk of convenience or illustrative selection.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This legal-institutional multiple-case docket study tracks the procedural history and post-judgment enforcement (cumprimento de sentença) of three Brazilian Public Civil Actions (ações civis públicas) demanding municipal sewerage infrastructure in Aquidauana (MS), Santa Maria (RS), and Tubarão (SC), drawn from the 258 lawsuits previously mapped in Barcellos (2014). Under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (structured non-validated judgment), the study is strong in legal source accuracy, jurisdictional specificity, procedural exposure definition, institutional context, and docket-level replicability: it documents exact docket numbers, judicial timelines, appellate delays, daily fine orders, and prosecutorial enforcement failures, notably exposing how the Aquidauana proceeding was formally extinguished as "fulfilled" in 2011 upon submission of a 30-year concession bill while actual municipal sewage coverage stood at 15%, and how Tubarão lacked sewerage implementation 12 years after filing. However, substantial methodological limitations restrict generalizability and causal inference: the selection of 3 cases from 258 is asserted to be "random" without any documented sampling method; docket synthesis relies on unpublished 2016 undergraduate chronicles without a standardized coding rubric; restricted online access to full court files in TJMS and TJRS limited documentary verification (and Santa Maria's 2012 compliance was inferred solely from judicial archiving without external physical audit); and the descriptive design lacks comparator municipalities or controls for concurrent concession renewals, licensing bottlenecks, and municipal politics.
raw_response.overall_rating: Strong legal-institutional docket documentation; high concern for selection, coding, and causal inference (structured non-validated judgment)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Doctrinal-empirical judicial docket-tracking multiple-case study (narrative procedural chronicle of three Public Civil Actions on municipal sanitation in Brazil, cross-referenced with secondary utility/news records)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research aims, case selection from Barcellos (2014), and narrative chronicle method are on PDF Pages 1-4 (Resumo, Abstract, Introdução, journal pp. 72-75); individual case chronicles and court portal/news triangulation are in Sections 1-3 on PDF Pages 4-16 (Aquidauana pp. 75-80, Santa Maria pp. 80-84, Tubarão pp. 84-87); comparative institutional synthesis and portal transparency findings are in Discussão and Conclusão on PDF Pages 16-20 (journal pp. 87-91).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study is a legal-institutional and empirical docket-tracking case study prepared by public law scholars analyzing judicial proceedings, court portal records, and concession documents across three sanitation lawsuits, without human-subject interviews/ethnography (making CASP Qualitative Checklist a poor fit for participant recruitment, reflexivity, and ethics items) and without non-litigated comparator units or statistical estimation (ruling out ROBINS-I, JBI checklists, and MMAT). The Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework directly evaluates its doctrinal accuracy, procedural/exposure operationalization, sampling from the 258-case universe, documentary measurement, and institutional enforcement context.
